To the General Convention of tlie Psi Upsilon Fraternity :

We, the undersigned, members of the 0. . Society of the University of
Minnesota, hereby respsetfuUy make application for a charter, to organize a
Chapter of the W. T. Fraternity. The action, as will be seen by the acoom-
;panjring memorial, is in accordance with the advice and approval of the alum
ni members of the If T. Fraternity, resident in Minnesota.
. That you may
have a proper knowledge of the character and condition of our society, we pre
sent the foUowing history, with a statement of some facts regarding the Uni
versity of Minnesota.
In January, 1879, Messrs. Keyser and RockweU of '79, determined to take
;the necessary steps to secure, if possible, the organization of a local society,
looking as its ultimate aim, to a connection with some leading eastern fratern
ity A meeting was held on the 8th of March 1879, at which were present
thirteen proposed members. At a subsequent meeting an organization was

perfected in accordance with a plan proposed. Among the provisions of the
constitution adopted, were pledges of secracy and of fidelity to the requirements
of this society, and regular semi-monthly literary meetings. Among the con
ditions requisite for the admission of new members were uprightness of charac
ter, high standing in scholarship, and an election to membership by a unani
mous vote of the active members.
Under the constitution, the 0, $. society has continued to exist, with its

original purpose ever in view. Additions have been made from time to time to

II. The average attendance at the University during the year 1880-81, is 276

It is the earnest intention of our members, to make the V. T. Chapter, if it .

EBCEPTION AT HON. PEEEY H. SMITH'S.

FoUowing the exercises at Central Hall the members of the Fraternity and
their friends were entertained by Hon. Perry H. Smith (Wi6), and Mrs.
"
Smith, at their beautiful residence on the North Side." It was a thoroughly
social and enjoyable affair. The decorations of the exterior and interior were
of a chaste and pleasing character. Upon the outside of the house on the
porches hung a number of Chinese lanterns. In the interior, facing the en
trance, there hung over the dining-room, pendant from vines of smilax, the
word "Welcome," in letters of carnations, upon an arched bed of white roses.
Over the parlor door was a double five-pointed floral star, whUe over the library
door hung the diamond-shaped badge of the Fraternity in carnations and white
roses. In the window of the Ubrary was a masterpiece of the florist's art, in
the shape of an arch over a bed of Jacqueminot and other rare roses, in which
was displayed the motto of the order, and the words "Psi UpsUon 1833."

Between the library and music-room there hung another double five-pointed
floral star. In the conservatory, with its rare plants and exotics in great vari
ety, where a fountain was playing, there were additional decorations in the
shape of various-colored candles and hanging Cninese lanterns. Mr. and Mrs.
Smith did the honors in the music-room, assisted by Miss Tierman, of Evanston, and Miss Helen Swing. There -were upwards of 500 ladies and gentlemen
present during the evening, and all were loud in tteir praises of the hospitaUty
of the host and hostess.
In the large baU-room on the upper floor dancing was enjoyed, and in the
bilUard-room an elegant colla,tion was served.
During the evening a number of the under-graduate members of the Fra
ternity assembled in one of the parlors, armed with the Prate nity song-books,
and entertained the guests and graduate members with some of the old songs
of the Fraternity,
"
singing "MeineBraut," "The JoUy Convocation," "Smok
ing Song," Joy of Psi UpsUon," and others. The boys were in good voice,
and their hearty rendition of these
inspiring coUege airs was highly enjoyed by
their audience.
